title: Amit Shah Sets 2029 Deadline for Uniform Civil Code in 21 NDA-Ruled States
excerpt: Speaking in Mumbai, the Union home minister said BJP-led NDA governments in 21 states would introduce a common civil code before the 2029 Lok Sabha elections, and announced a month-long campaign marking Narendra Modi's 25 years in public life.
body:
• Union Home Minister Amit Shah said Sunday that all 21 states governed by the BJP-led NDA will implement the Uniform Civil Code before the 2029 general elections.
  • Uttarakhand became the first state to pass a UCC law in February 2024 and remains the only state where it is fully in force; Gujarat and Assam passed their bills in 2026, and Madhya Pradesh's cabinet approved the measure last month.
  • Shah framed the pledge alongside a hardline security posture, citing the surgical strikes, air strikes and Operation Sindoor as evidence of a "zero tolerance" approach to terrorism.
  • He also announced a month-long "Seva Sankalp Abhiyan" from September 17 to October 17 marking Prime Minister Narendra Modi's 25 years in public life.

Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Sunday set a firm deadline for one of the BJP's longest-standing ideological commitments, declaring that the Uniform Civil Code will be implemented in all 21 states governed by the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance before the 2029 Lok Sabha elections. Speaking at an event in Mumbai, Shah said the government had already introduced the code in several states and was confident of completing the rollout across every NDA-ruled jurisdiction within the current government's term.

"We introduced the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) in several states. I am confident that we will implement the UCC in all 21 states governed by the BJP-led NDA before 2029."

— Amit Shah, Union Home Minister

What the Uniform Civil Code would do

The Uniform Civil Code would replace the separate religion-based personal laws that currently govern marriage, divorce, inheritance, adoption and succession for different communities with a single legal framework applying to all citizens regardless of faith. Supporters argue that a common code advances gender equality and constitutional uniformity; critics say it intrudes on religious freedom and personal tradition.

The BJP has carried the UCC in its election manifestos for decades, and Shah presented the pledge as part of the government's broader reform record. He cited the abolition of triple talaq, saying it had given Muslim women equal rights, and pointed to the introduction of the code in several states as evidence that the rollout was already underway.

Where the rollout stands

Uttarakhand led the way in February 2024, becoming the first state to pass a UCC law; the code has been in force there since January 2025, making it the only state where implementation is complete. Gujarat followed with a bill passed in March 2026, while Assam became the first northeastern state to pass UCC legislation in May 2026. Last month, Madhya Pradesh's cabinet unanimously approved the measure at a special meeting in Bhopal's Jagdishpura.

Gujarat, Assam and Madhya Pradesh are still awaiting presidential assent and formal notification. Three more states — Maharashtra, West Bengal and Chhattisgarh — have formed committees to prepare drafts, meaning the pipeline of states backing the measure now extends beyond the core BJP-ruled states into states with more contested politics.

Security, courts and the political calendar

Shah used the Mumbai appearance to review 12 years of the Modi government's record. He credited the criminal-justice overhaul under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita with raising conviction rates by roughly 30 per cent in a single year in several states, and said work was underway toward a system in which cases receive justice within three years.

On national security, he said surgical strikes, air strikes and Operation Sindoor had established a policy of "zero tolerance" toward terrorism and that India's security posture had been fundamentally transformed.

A quieter note on dialogue

Responding to questions about Gen Z-led movements, language disputes and the proposed National Register of Citizens in Manipur, Shah said discussions were underway and decisions would be announced once allies and state leaders agreed. "We are in a democracy. People hold different views on various issues, and it is essential that those views are expressed," he said. "We believe in dialogue and discussion."

The view from the diaspora

For NRIs with property and family ties in India, the pledge matters beyond politics: inheritance and succession of Indian assets are currently governed by different personal laws, and a single framework could simplify estate matters for families with members across religions and jurisdictions. But with assent and notification still pending in most adopting states, any practical change is years away.

What's next

The immediate tests for the 2029 pledge are procedural: presidential assent for the Gujarat, Assam and Madhya Pradesh laws, draft reports from the three committee states, and the legal challenges the measure is almost certain to draw. With the next general election three years away, the UCC now has a concrete deadline — and with it, a yardstick the opposition will hold the government to.
